title: Learning: Only What Was Asked
text: A wine shop needs to know a customer is over 18. The customer holds a digital ID with a name, an address and a date of birth.
held: The shop learned one fact. It could not have written down anything else if it wanted to.

cards.label: Prove “over 18” from the ID, revealing nothing else
Show the whole ID
cards.why: The shop needed one fact and now holds a name, an address and a birth date it has to protect for ever.

cards.label: Reject the proof
cards.why: Nothing was wrong with it. Refusing something legitimate without looking is its own failure: check, then act.

fields.label: rests on a credential from
fields.check: Check which issuer's signature the proof rests on
fields.ok: A credential signed by the ID issuer you trust.

intrusion.value: an issuer nobody has heard of
intrusion.detail: The underlying credential was signed by an unknown issuer.
intrusion.why: A flawless proof about a credential from a made-up issuer shows only that someone made up an issuer.
intrusion.reveal: The proof rested on a credential from an issuer the Verifier does not trust.

temptations.label: Ask for the date of birth too, for your records
temptations.why: The proof exists so that you don't hold it. Data you never collected can't leak.

cards.label: Complete the sale and note who the customer was
cards.why: There is nothing to note: the proof carried no identity. Trying to attach one rebuilds what it removed.

teaches: Selective disclosure: prove the one fact, reveal none of the rest.
A proof is only as good as the credential under it. Check the issuer.
The safest personal data is the data you never receive.
